_note: Fictional composite diagnostic-reasoning cases for the psychiatry clerkship. Do not include PHI. These cases teach reasoning structure, not patient-specific diagnosis or treatment advice.

cases.title: Mania, Psychosis, Or Substance-Induced?
cases.learnerGoal: Build a problem representation, keep substance and medical causes in the differential, and update without anchoring.
cases.patientBrief: A 24-year-old is admitted after four nights of little sleep, pressured speech, grand plans, irritability, and hearing the voice of God. A roommate reports heavy cannabis use and one recent stimulant exposure.

facts.label: Timeline
facts.text: Symptoms escalated over one week after several nights of decreased sleep.

facts.label: MSE
facts.text: Pressured speech, flight of ideas, grandiosity, irritable affect, and poor insight.

facts.label: Safety
facts.text: Tried to leave the ED to meet investors at 2 AM; no clear suicidal intent.

facts.label: Collateral
facts.text: Roommate reports cannabis most days and one stimulant pill at a party.

steps.title: Problem Representation
steps.prompt: Which one-liner best captures the syndrome without prematurely closing?

choices.text: Young adult with acute decreased need for sleep, increased energy, grandiosity, pressured speech, psychosis, and substance exposure.
choices.feedback: Best. It names the time course, manic syndrome, psychotic features, and the substance exposure that still needs interpretation.

choices.text: Young adult with schizophrenia because there are auditory hallucinations.
choices.feedback: This anchors on one symptom. Hallucinations can occur in mania, substances, delirium, trauma, and medical illness.

choices.text: Cannabis-induced psychosis until proven otherwise.
choices.feedback: Substances matter, but the decreased sleep, energy, pressured speech, and grandiosity point to a manic syndrome that cannot be collapsed into cannabis alone.

steps.title: Differential
steps.prompt: What should be highest on the working differential right now?

choices.text: Bipolar I disorder, current manic episode with psychotic features; rule out substance-induced and medical causes.
choices.feedback: Best. It keeps the leading syndrome and the required rule-outs in view.

choices.text: Primary psychotic disorder only.
choices.feedback: A primary psychotic disorder remains possible, but the manic syndrome is too prominent to ignore.

choices.text: Personality disorder with attention-seeking behavior.
choices.feedback: This is stigmatizing and misses a potentially severe mood episode with safety implications.

steps.title: Update With New Data
steps.prompt: Collateral later confirms a prior week-long episode of decreased sleep and impulsive spending without substances. How should you update?

choices.text: Increase confidence in bipolar spectrum illness while still documenting substance contribution and medical rule-out.
choices.feedback: Best. Prior similar episodes shift the probability toward bipolar illness without pretending substances are irrelevant.

choices.text: Ignore the substance history because bipolar disorder is now certain.
choices.feedback: Do not convert probability into certainty. Substance use still affects risk, management, and discharge planning.

choices.text: Keep the original substance-induced diagnosis because tox was positive.
choices.feedback: A positive tox screen is a clue, not a complete explanation. Timeline and recurrence change the formulation.

steps.title: Supervised Next Step
steps.prompt: What is the student's best next contribution on rounds?

choices.text: Present the manic syndrome, safety risks, substance/medical rule-outs, sleep restoration need, and questions for collateral.
choices.feedback: Best. The student adds value by making the reasoning explicit and showing what would change the working diagnosis.

choices.text: Recommend a specific medication dose.
choices.feedback: Students should not independently prescribe. Focus on formulation, risks, monitoring questions, and supervised treatment reasoning.

choices.text: Wait for the attending to decide the diagnosis.
choices.feedback: The point is not independent certainty. It is supervised reasoning that the team can critique and improve.

biasChecks: Do not anchor on the tox screen.
Do not treat hallucinations as synonymous with schizophrenia.
Separate syndrome, likely diagnosis, contributors, and treatment targets.

cases.title: Delirium Or New Psychosis?
cases.setting: Consult question on a medical floor
cases.learnerGoal: Use attention, arousal, acuity, and fluctuation to avoid mislabeling delirium as primary psychosis.
cases.patientBrief: A 72-year-old post-op patient says insects are crawling on the wall. Nursing reports waxing and waning confusion, poor sleep, new urinary symptoms, and recent diphenhydramine.

facts.label: Timeline
facts.text: New confusion began two days after surgery and fluctuates across the day.

facts.label: Attention
facts.text: Cannot recite months backward and drifts off during the interview.

facts.label: Perception
facts.text: Reports vivid visual hallucinations, worse at night.

facts.label: Medication
facts.text: Received opioid analgesia and diphenhydramine for sleep.

steps.title: Most Diagnostic Cue
steps.prompt: Which cue most strongly changes your reasoning?

choices.text: Fluctuating inattention and altered arousal.
choices.feedback: Best. Acute fluctuating inattention is the anchor for delirium.

choices.text: The patient reports hallucinations.
choices.feedback: Hallucinations matter, but visual hallucinations with inattention and fluctuation should push delirium high.

choices.text: The patient is older.
choices.feedback: Age increases risk, but diagnosis rests on clinical features and time course, not age alone.

steps.title: Syndrome Frame
steps.prompt: What syndrome should lead the working formulation?

choices.text: Delirium, likely multifactorial, with medication and infection contributors to evaluate.
choices.feedback: Best. It frames the syndrome as medical until proven otherwise.

choices.text: Late-onset schizophrenia.
choices.feedback: Late-onset psychosis exists, but this presentation is acute, fluctuating, inattentive, and medically loaded.

choices.text: Dementia progression.
choices.feedback: Dementia can increase delirium vulnerability, but sudden fluctuation suggests delirium over baseline neurocognitive disorder.

steps.title: Rule Out First
steps.prompt: What should the student emphasize to the team?

choices.text: Review deliriogenic medications, check infection/metabolic/hypoxia contributors, and use reorientation/sleep-wake measures.
choices.feedback: Best. The student can help by organizing causes and nonpharmacologic prevention.

choices.text: Start by asking whether the hallucinations are mood-congruent.
choices.feedback: That question can matter in mood psychosis, but delirium features should be addressed first.

choices.text: Ask for a standing benzodiazepine because the patient is anxious.
choices.feedback: Benzodiazepines usually worsen non-withdrawal delirium. Escalate dangerous agitation under supervision and local policy.

biasChecks: Do not let hallucinations override the attention exam.
Do not call a patient psychotic before assessing acuity and fluctuation.
Ask what changed from baseline and when.

cases.title: Catatonia Or Refusal?
cases.learnerGoal: Describe motor signs objectively and avoid interpreting catatonia as oppositional behavior.
cases.patientBrief: A patient with severe depression is mute, staring, barely eating, and holding an awkward arm posture. Staff wonder if the patient is refusing care.

facts.label: Motor
facts.text: Staring, immobility, posturing, and possible waxy flexibility.

facts.label: Speech
facts.text: Mute through most of the interview.

facts.label: Risk
facts.text: Poor oral intake and reduced mobility.

facts.label: Context
facts.text: Severe mood episode with psychotic guilt themes earlier in admission.

steps.title: Chart Language
steps.prompt: Which documentation phrase best supports diagnostic reasoning?

choices.text: Mute, immobile, staring, posturing, and minimally responsive; screen for catatonia with BFCRS.
choices.feedback: Best. It describes observable signs and links them to a structured assessment.

choices.text: Patient is uncooperative and refusing to participate.
choices.feedback: This moralizes the behavior and can delay recognition of a treatable motor syndrome.

choices.text: Patient seems depressed.
choices.feedback: Depression may be the underlying illness, but the motor syndrome needs its own assessment.

steps.title: First Reasoning Move
steps.prompt: What is the safest supervised next step?

choices.text: Raise catatonia with the team, trend vitals/intake, use BFCRS, and discuss lorazepam challenge per protocol.
choices.feedback: Best. It combines recognition, measurement, medical monitoring, and supervised treatment reasoning.

choices.text: Recommend antipsychotic escalation because psychotic depression is possible.
choices.feedback: Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia or malignant catatonia/NMS. Exclude catatonia before that move.

choices.text: Wait until the patient chooses to engage.
choices.feedback: Catatonia can be life-threatening. Waiting can worsen dehydration, immobility, and malignant progression.

choices.text: This is concerning for catatonia; we need structured assessment and medical rule-out before treating it as refusal or psychosis alone.
choices.feedback: Best. It is clear, humble, and action-oriented.

choices.text: This is definitely malignant catatonia.
choices.feedback: Malignant catatonia must be considered if autonomic instability appears, but do not overstate what is not present.

choices.text: Catatonia is rare, so it is unlikely.
choices.feedback: Catatonia is under-recognized and occurs across mood, psychotic, autistic, and medical conditions.

biasChecks: Avoid labeling motor symptoms as refusal.
Ask whether antipsychotics could worsen the syndrome.
Track intake, mobility, vitals, and objective motor signs.

cases.title: Crisis, Trauma, Mood, Or Personality?
cases.learnerGoal: Separate symptoms, syndrome, diagnosis, formulation, and treatment targets without stigmatizing.
cases.patientBrief: A 28-year-old admitted after self-injury following a breakup reports chronic emptiness, childhood trauma, nightmares, mood reactivity, and intermittent suicidal thoughts.

facts.label: Safety
facts.text: Self-injury escalated after perceived abandonment; suicidal thoughts fluctuate.

facts.label: Trauma
facts.text: Nightmares, hypervigilance, and avoidance since childhood abuse.

facts.label: Mood
facts.text: Mood shifts over hours with interpersonal stress; no clear sustained manic episode.

facts.label: Function
facts.text: Longstanding unstable relationships and intense fear of rejection.

steps.title: Separate The Layers
steps.prompt: Which formulation best separates the clinical layers?

choices.text: Current safety crisis with trauma symptoms and borderline personality traits; evaluate depressive disorder and focus treatment targets on safety, affect regulation, sleep, and follow-up.
choices.feedback: Best. It keeps risk, trauma, personality pattern, differential diagnosis, and treatment targets distinct.

choices.text: Borderline patient acting out after a breakup.
choices.feedback: This is stigmatizing and collapses the person into a label. It also misses trauma and mood differential.

choices.text: Major depression only because suicidal thoughts are present.
choices.feedback: Depression must be assessed, but suicidality is not specific to major depression.

steps.title: Manage Uncertainty
steps.prompt: What uncertainty should you explicitly carry forward?

choices.text: Whether depressive, PTSD, substance, and personality factors are all contributing to risk and what changes with time and collateral.
choices.feedback: Best. Psychiatric formulation often tracks multiple contributors rather than forcing one premature diagnosis.

choices.text: Whether the patient is being manipulative.
choices.feedback: This framing is pejorative and not clinically precise. Replace it with needs, fears, functions, risks, and skills deficits.

choices.text: Whether the patient really has trauma.
choices.feedback: Do not make disbelief the central uncertainty. Clarify symptoms, impact, safety, and treatment needs.

choices.text: I am separating the acute safety target from the longer-term formulation: today we need suicide risk, coping plan, sleep, and follow-up; diagnostically I am considering PTSD, MDD, and borderline personality traits.
choices.feedback: Best. It shows diagnostic humility and connects formulation to immediate inpatient work.

choices.text: This is a classic borderline case.
choices.feedback: This sounds dismissive and does not tell the team what to do today.

choices.text: The diagnosis is unclear, so I do not have a plan.
choices.feedback: Uncertainty is not paralysis. You can still name treatment targets and what data would update the formulation.

biasChecks: Do not use diagnosis as a shorthand for blame.
Separate acute safety targets from longitudinal formulation.
Carry more than one contributor when the case genuinely has more than one.
